title: Similar matrices
objectives: Recognise similar matrices and what they share: eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank.
Say which quantities change with the basis, such as eigenvectors and entries.
Tell similar matrices from matrices that only share eigenvalues.

screens.title: The same map in a new grid
screens.prose: The map $\mathbf{A}$ is written in the standard grid. Describe the same map in a new grid whose steps are the columns of $\mathbf{M}$. $\mathbf{M}$ turns new coordinates into standard ones, $\mathbf{A}$ acts, and $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ turns the result back: $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{B}$.

hints.text: Do $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ first, then multiply by $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$.
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ has rows $(4, 5)$ and $(2, 5)$.
$\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ subtracts row 2 from row 1, so row 1 becomes $(4 - 2, 5 - 5) = (2, 0)$. Row 2 stays $(2, 5)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$, then let $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ subtract row 2 from row 1.

byKey.r0c1: Row 1 of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ is $(4, 5)$ and row 2 is $(2, 5)$. $4 - 2 = 2$.
byKey.r0c2: Row 1 of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ minus row 2 is $(5 - 5) = 0$. The shear in $\mathbf{M}$ has cancelled that entry.
byKey.r1c1: Row 2 of $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ is row 2 of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$, which starts with $2$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting row 2 from row 1 gives $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$. Same map, new grid, different entries.

screens.title: One arrow, two grids
screens.prose: The grid now follows the columns of $\mathbf{M}$. Drag $\mathbf{u}$ and read its coordinates in both grids. $\mathbf{u} = (2, 2)$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}$ with eigenvalue 5.
screens.question: At $\mathbf{u} = (2, 2)$ the new coordinates are $(0, 2)$. What does $\mathbf{B}$ do to $(0, 2)$?

options.text: It gives $(0, 10)$: the new coordinates of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$

options.why: $(10, 10)$ is $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ in the standard grid. The caption reads it in the new grid as $(0, 10)$.
$\mathbf{u}$ is stretched by 5 whichever grid you use. A change of grid cannot undo the stretch.
That is $\mathbf{B}(0, 1)$, the second column of $\mathbf{B}$. Your arrow is $(0, 2)$, twice as long.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption for $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ in the new grid.

explain.text: In the new grid $\mathbf{u}$ is $(0, 2)$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ is $(0, 10)$. Column 2 of $\mathbf{B}$ is $(0, 5)$, so $\mathbf{B}$ stretches this arrow by 5 too.

screens.title: Same eigenvalues, new entries
screens.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalues 5 and 2, with trace 7 and determinant 10. $\mathbf{B}$ looks quite different. Find its eigenvalues from $\det(\mathbf{B} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = 0$.
screens.question: What are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{B}$?

hints.text: For this $\mathbf{B}$, $\det(\mathbf{B} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = (2 - \lambda)(5 - \lambda)$, because the top right entry is 0.
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.
$(2 - \lambda)(5 - \lambda) = 0$ gives $\lambda = 2$ and $\lambda = 5$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{B}$ has eigenvalues 5 and 2 again, and also trace 7 and determinant 10. No entry of $\mathbf{B}$ matches $\mathbf{A}$, yet the spectrum does. Matrices linked by $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ are called **similar**.

screens.title: Similar, and the best case
screens.prose: $\mathbf{B}$ is **similar** to $\mathbf{A}$ when $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ for some invertible $\mathbf{M}$. Diagonalising was a case of this, with $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{X}$.
screens.question: Which matrix is similar to $\mathbf{A}$?

options.why: You put the trace and determinant on the diagonal. Similar matrices share those numbers, but the diagonal holds the eigenvalues.
That is $2\mathbf{A}$. Doubling a matrix doubles its eigenvalues to 10 and 4, so it is not similar to $\mathbf{A}$.
This has trace 10, but $\mathbf{A}$ has trace 7. Similar matrices must have equal traces.

hints.text: $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$ is already on the canvas.
Compare the trace of each option with the trace of $\mathbf{A}$, which is 7.
Only $\mathrm{diag}(5, 2)$ has trace 7 and determinant 10, and it equals $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A similar matrix has the same trace, 7, and the same determinant, 10.

byKey.tracedet: You copied the trace and determinant onto the diagonal. The diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ holds 5 and 2.

explain.text: With $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{X}$, the product $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$ is $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$. Diagonalisation is the best choice of $\mathbf{M}$: it makes the similar matrix diagonal.

screens.prose: Compare $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ with $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$. Which properties does a change of grid keep?
screens.question: Select all that apply: which must every pair of similar matrices share?

options.why: $\mathbf{B}(1, 1) = (2, 7)$, which is not a multiple of $(1, 1)$. Eigenvectors move to $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$.
$\mathbf{A}$ has 4 and $\mathbf{B}$ has 2. Entries describe the grid, not the map.

hints.text: Test each property on the two matrices shown.
Trace and determinant are the sum and product of the eigenvalues.
Eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank agree. Eigenvectors and entries do not.

feedback.correct: Eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank survive. Eigenvectors and entries do not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each property on the pair: does it agree for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$?

byKey.vec: You kept the eigenvector. It is $\mathbf{M}^{-1}(1, 1) = (0, 1)$ for $\mathbf{B}$.
byKey.entry: You kept an entry. Only quantities of the map itself survive.

explain.text: The trace and determinant come from the eigenvalues, so they survive. Rank survives because $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ are invertible. Eigenvectors and entries depend on the grid.

screens.title: Where the eigenvector goes
screens.prose: If $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 5\mathbf{x}$, then $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 5\,\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$. So the eigenvector moves to $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$.
screens.question: Find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ for $\mathbf{x} = (1, 1)$.

hints.text: Multiply each row of $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ by $\mathbf{x}$.
Row 1 is $(1, -1)$ and row 2 is $(0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: $(0, 1)$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{B}$ with eigenvalue 5: $\mathbf{B}(0, 1) = (0, 5)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take row 1 $(1, -1)$ and row 2 $(0, 1)$ of $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ against $(1, 1)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{M}^{-1}(1, 1) = (0, 1)$, the direction of the new coordinates $(0, 2)$ you saw. The eigenvalue 5 stays; the eigenvector changes with the grid.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ rotates every arrow by 90 degrees. Then $\det(\mathbf{R} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = \lambda^2 + 1$.
screens.question: What are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{R}$?

options.text: $i$ and $-i$: complex, with no real eigenvector

options.why: You solved $\lambda^2 = 1$. The equation is $\lambda^2 + 1 = 0$, which has no real root.

options.text: None: the matrix has no eigenvalues at all
options.why: A $2 \times 2$ matrix always has two eigenvalues. Here they are complex.
You read the entries of $\mathbf{R}$ as eigenvalues. Eigenvalues come from the determinant equation.

hints.text: Solve $\lambda^2 + 1 = 0$.
A real number squared is never negative.
$\lambda^2 = -1$ gives $\lambda = i$ and $\lambda = -i$.

feedback.correct: $\lambda = \pm i$. Their sum is the trace 0, and their product is the determinant 1.

byKey.pm1: You solved $\lambda^2 = 1$ and lost the plus sign in $\lambda^2 + 1$.
byKey.none: Two roots always exist, but here they are not real.

explain.text: A rotation keeps no direction, so it has no real eigenvector. Its eigenvalues are a conjugate pair, $i$ and $-i$, and they still add to the trace and multiply to the determinant. A real symmetric matrix can never do this (lesson 5).

screens.prose: $\mathbf{C} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $2\mathbf{I}$ both have eigenvalues 2 and 2, trace 4, determinant 4 and rank 2.
screens.question: Are $\mathbf{C}$ and $2\mathbf{I}$ similar?

options.text: Yes: they share eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank
options.why: You checked only the shared properties. They are necessary for similarity, not enough.
$\mathbf{C}^{-1}(2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{C} = 2\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{C} = 2\mathbf{I}$. It never produces $\mathbf{C}$.
Scaling changes the eigenvalues. Similarity keeps them fixed.

hints.text: Try to build $\mathbf{C}$ as $\mathbf{M}^{-1}(2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{M}$ for any $\mathbf{M}$.
The scalar 2 comes out of the product.
$\mathbf{M}^{-1}(2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{M} = 2\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{M} = 2\mathbf{I}$, whatever $\mathbf{M}$ is.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out $\mathbf{M}^{-1}(2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{M}$ and see what it can equal.

byKey.yes: You compared eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank. Two matrices can agree on all four and still not be similar.
byKey.pick: You tried one $\mathbf{M}$. The product is $2\mathbf{I}$ for every $\mathbf{M}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{C}$ has one eigen-direction, like the shear in lesson 3, so it cannot be diagonalised. $2\mathbf{I}$ is already diagonal. A matrix similar to a diagonal one is diagonalisable, so the two cannot be similar.

screens.prose: Show that $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ has the same characteristic polynomial as $\mathbf{A}$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $= \det(\mathbf{M}^{-1}(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{M})$, taking $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{M}$ out of both terms
$= \det(\mathbf{M}^{-1})\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\det(\mathbf{M})$, since $\det$ of a product is the product of the $\det$s

hints.text: Start by writing $\mathbf{B}$ in full. Then make $\lambda\mathbf{I}$ look like $\mathbf{M}^{-1}(\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{M}$.
Factor out before you split the determinant.
Substitute, insert $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{M}$, factor, split the product, cancel.

feedback.correct: The characteristic polynomials are equal, so the eigenvalues, trace and determinant are too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line should follow from the one before.

byKey.fac: You factor only after $\lambda\mathbf{I}$ has been rewritten as $\lambda\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{M}$.
byKey.prod: You can split the determinant only once the product is factored.

explain.text: Equal polynomials have equal roots, so $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ share their eigenvalues with multiplicities. The trace is their sum and the determinant their product. That is the proof behind what you saw with $\mathbf{B}$.

screens.title: A case where eigenvalues are enough
screens.prose: Edge case. Let $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Y}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Y}^{-1}$ share one $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$. Then $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$, so $$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}^{-1}\,\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}^{-1}.$$ Two diagonalisable matrices with the same eigenvalues are always similar.
screens.question: Write $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$. Which $\mathbf{M}$ is it?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$, the outer factor on the left. You need the matrix on the right of $\mathbf{A}$.
Neither factor is inverted here, so $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{-1}$ do not pair up.
This puts the inverse on $\mathbf{X}$, but $\mathbf{A}$ is sandwiched as $\mathbf{X}\ldots\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ in the other order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read off the right-hand factor of $\mathbf{A}$ in the displayed line.

explain.text: The factor on the right of $\mathbf{A}$ is $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}^{-1}$, and its inverse $\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ sits on the left. This is why eigenvalues, with diagonalisability, decide similarity. Without diagonalisability, they do not.

screens.title: One risk model, two coordinate systems
screens.prose: Weekly returns on two assets have covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ in $\%^2$. A second desk uses the orthogonal factors $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1, -2)$. Its matrix is $\mathbf{Q}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{Q} = \mathrm{diag}(6, 1)$.
screens.question: Asset 1 has variance 5. What is the variance of asset 2?

widget.label: Variance of asset 2
widget.accept: 2: the total variance 6 + 1 = 7 is the trace, the same in both coordinates.

hints.text: Which quantity does not change with the grid?
For an orthogonal $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{Q}^T = \mathbf{Q}^{-1}$, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_f$ is similar to $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
The traces agree: $5 + v_2 = 6 + 1$, so $v_2 = 2$.

feedback.correct: $7 - 5 = 2$. Total variance is the same in both coordinates.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Similar matrices have equal traces: add the diagonal of each.

byKey.factor: 1 is the variance of the second factor, not of asset 2. Entries depend on the coordinates.
byKey.first: 5 is asset 1's variance. Use the trace to get asset 2's.
byKey.six: 6 is the first factor's variance. The two desks use different coordinates.

explain.text: The eigenvalues 6 and 1, and the total variance 7, are the numbers worth reporting. Entries need the coordinates named. For non-orthogonal portfolios $\mathbf{M}$ the covariance becomes $\mathbf{M}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{M}$, which is not similar to $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$: with $\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ its trace is 16, not 7.

ideas: $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}$ is the same map in a new grid; we call $\mathbf{B}$ similar to $\mathbf{A}$.
Similar matrices share eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank. Eigenvectors and entries change with the grid.
Equal eigenvalues are not enough: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is not similar to $2\mathbf{I}$. Diagonalisable matrices with equal eigenvalues are similar.

formula.name: Similarity
formula.note: The eigenvalue stays. The eigenvector becomes $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$.

summary.trap: Sharing eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank does not make two matrices similar.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues, and $\mathbf{B}$ has the same ones.

byKey.sum: 7 is the trace. The determinant multiplies the eigenvalues.

explain.text: Similar matrices share eigenvalues, so $\mathbf{B}$ has eigenvalues 3 and 4. The determinant is their product, 12.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{P}$ has trace 5 and determinant 6. Four other matrices are listed by their eigenvalues.
quiz.question: Which of these cannot be similar to $\mathbf{P}$?

options.why: These have trace 5 and determinant 6, and distinct eigenvalues, so the matrix is similar to $\mathbf{P}$.
Its eigenvalues are 3 and 2: trace 5, determinant 6. It is similar to $\mathbf{P}$.
Trace 5 and determinant 6 again, so it is similar.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{P}$ has eigenvalues 2 and 3. Compare the traces.

explain.text: $\mathbf{P}$ has eigenvalues 2 and 3 ($\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6$). Eigenvalues 1 and 6 give trace 7, so they cannot be similar.

quiz.question: What is the product of its two eigenvalues?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The product of the eigenvalues is the determinant of $\mathbf{R}$.

byKey.zero: Complex eigenvalues still multiply to the determinant, which is 1.

explain.text: The determinant of $\mathbf{R}$ is $0 \times 0 - (-1)(1) = 1$. The product of the eigenvalues must equal it, even when they are complex.

quiz.prose: A $2 \times 2$ matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is diagonalisable and both its eigenvalues are 3.
quiz.question: What is $\mathbf{A}$?

options.why: This has one eigen-direction, so it cannot be diagonalised.
Trace 6 allows many eigenvalue pairs, such as 1 and 5.
$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}(3\mathbf{I})\mathbf{X}^{-1} = 3\mathbf{I}$ settles it.
